sections.html: Mandan is both the seat and the biggest city of Morton County, which reaches along the Missouri River in south-central North Dakota. About 33,291 people lived here in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 34,601. Bismarck and Burleigh County lie across the river as part of the same metro area. The tax offices are in Mandan, so a seller near the river should check which side the parcel is on before looking anything up.

sections.h2: Who values property in the county
sections.html:
Valuation is split between two offices. Unincorporated land, plus any city or township that contracts with the county, goes through the county Tax Equalization Office. Inside Mandan, the city's own Assessing and Building Inspections departments do the work.

Market value as of February 1 each year drives residential and commercial assessments. Farmland uses the state's agricultural valuation guide instead. Ten zones cover the county, which means each property is reassessed at least once a decade. When your zone comes up, you get a letter offering either an assessor appointment or a property detail sheet to complete.

Permits follow a similar split. The county Building Inspector covers unincorporated areas, plus Almont and Glen Ullin on request. Flasher, Hebron and New Salem each issue their own.

sections.h2: Credits that can lower a bill
sections.html:
Three programs reduce residential tax in Morton County, and each depends on the owner's situation.

  • Homestead Property Tax Credit: owners 65 or older, or disabled, whose household income stays at or under $70,000 after medical deductions
  • Disabled veteran property tax credit: a disability rating of 50 percent or more
  • Primary Residence Credit, run by the State Tax Commissioner

The Tax Equalization Office also provides a property tax calculator and a farm residence exemption page. If you plan to sell, mention a credit you currently claim, since the buyer will not carry it over automatically.

Go to 210 2nd Ave NW, Mandan, ND 58554, or call 701-667-3310 to reach the Morton County Treasurer. Hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., holidays excepted. This elected office, with a four-year term, collects real estate and mobile home tax, mails statements and delinquent notices, and gives lenders the numbers for escrow accounts.

The bill is due January 1 and costs nothing extra through March 1. Settle the full year by February 15 and it falls by 5 percent. Here is the calendar:

DateEvent
February 1Valuation date
AprilCity or township board of equalization
Early JuneCounty board of equalization
AugustState board of equalization
By December 26Statements mailed
February 155% discount deadline
March 1First installment due
October 15Second installment due

Late charges come from section 57-20-01 of the Century Code. They start at 3 percent after March 1 and grow by 3 percent on May 1, July 1 and October 15. A second installment left past October 15 costs 6 percent.

Phone the assessor right away and ask for a review. Many questions end there without a hearing. The assessment letter shows each property's proposed true and full value, so compare it with what similar homes nearby have sold for.

If a call does not fix it, go to the local equalization meetings, which deal with the current year's value. Cities and townships meet in April, the Morton County Board of Equalization in early June, and the State Board of Equalization finishes its review in August. The state board can lower a value only for owners who appeared at both the local and county boards.

An abatement request is another option. It can cover the current and previous years, the deadline is November 1, and the applicant carries the burden of proof. Call the office to confirm which year applies. Forms come from the State Tax Commissioner's site or the county.

A parcel whose taxes, specials and interest remain unpaid in the third year can go to tax lien foreclosure. The county auditor follows each one, sends word to interested parties and holds one sale every year.

  • Before June 1: a foreclosure notice goes to the owner, occupants and others with an interest.
  • Before August 1: a notice of delinquent property is published in the official county newspaper.
  • October 1, 5 p.m.: everything owed must be paid to the County Treasurer.
  • After October 1: the owner can still pay in full before the sale starts.
  • Third Tuesday of November: the annual sale.

The sale itself is announced at least 15 days early in the auditor's office and on the county website, and at least 10 days early in the county newspaper.

You can sell and pay the tax out of the proceeds, and a cash buyer can often close faster than a lender-financed buyer. The title company asks the Treasurer for the payoff and pays it at closing.

The delinquency calendar is the reason to move early. After a county takes a tax deed, an owner can buy the property back only before it is resold, either in full or under an installment contract with at least 25 percent paid in cash. A tax foreclosure can also wipe out a mortgage, because the tax lien comes first.

Before you set a closing date:

  • Call the Treasurer at 701-667-3310 for a payoff that covers the whole year.
  • Find out whether any credit you claim ends with the sale.
  • Check the delinquency calendar to see how close the parcel is to October 1.
  • Tell the title company whether the house is inside Mandan or in the county, so the right assessor is contacted.

We buy Morton County houses as they are, including homes in Mandan and the smaller towns, and we work with your title company on the county payoff.

sections.h2: What to bring when you call
sections.html:
Whether you phone the Treasurer, the Tax Equalization Office or the City of Mandan, the first question will be which parcel you mean. Have the address and the parcel number from your latest statement in front of you. If you inherited the property, have the estate paperwork handy, because the person on the phone may need to confirm who is allowed to receive information.

Write down the answers as you go. For the Treasurer, you want the amount owed for the whole year and the date the figure runs through. For the assessor, you want the proposed true and full value and the zone the property is in. For a lender, you want the escrow balance, since the treasurer's office supplies figures to lenders for those accounts.

A lender-financed buyer needs an appraisal and loan approval, and either can slow the closing. A cash buyer skips both, which helps when the delinquency calendar is close or you need to be out of the house by a certain date.

The county still gets paid in full at closing in either case. The difference is who else has to say yes before the deed changes hands. With a cash purchase there is no loan underwriter in the middle, and no repair negotiation after an inspection, because the buyer prices the condition into the offer from the start.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Morton County?
faqs.a: The Morton County Treasurer, at 210 2nd Ave NW in Mandan. The phone is 701-667-3310.

faqs.q: Does Mandan assess its own property?
faqs.a: Yes. Mandan runs its own assessing and building inspection departments inside city limits. The county assesses unincorporated areas and towns that contract with it.

faqs.q: When is Morton County property tax due?
faqs.a: The tax is due January 1 and payable without penalty until March 1. A full payment by February 15 earns 5 percent off, and the second installment date is October 15.

faqs.q: When does Morton County foreclose tax liens?
faqs.a: The foreclosure date is October 1 at 5 p.m. The annual sale of delinquent property is the third Tuesday of November.

faqs.q: Which credits can reduce a Morton County bill?
faqs.a: The Homestead Credit, the disabled veteran credit and the Primary Residence Credit. The homestead income limit is $70,000 after medical deductions.
